searches.note: Nineteen searches of a share of twenty eight, nine left unspent for the run's shared allowance; one further call was refused by the search tool for a blocked domain before any search ran and is not counted. Most were restricted to the VDP's, wein.plus's or a house's own domain and read as summaries. Writers' own sites that came up were read and never cited. No fetch tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

The searches went first to the people (who of each family is living or dead), then to the dates the stories turn on (1950, 1982 and 1994 at Meyer-Näkel; 1578, 1900 and 2005 at Stodden; 1714 at Adeneuer; 1574, 1868, 1952, 1980 and 2020 at Deutzerhof; 1953, 1994, 2000 and 2024 at Kreuzberg), then to the sites on the VDP's own pages, then to the proposed swap.
The finding that matters most: Werner Näkel, held living by the author, died in September 2025, so he is now named with his dates.

tested: 1950 and the double name: wein.plus and the vieduvin profile give the founding by marriage of a Näkel to a Meyer, with 1.5 hectares; kept as the year the estate took its present shape.

The founder's son: Meininger, wein.plus magazine, Falstaff and the Rhein-Zeitung report his death in September 2025; Meininger gives 13 September aged 72 and one summary his birth in 1953; his takeover in 1982 from teaching is in wein.plus and Meininger; the VDP's pin of honour of 2023 on the VDP's own page.
VDP membership 1994: the VDP's estate page and the obituaries agree.
The Pfarrwingert: the VDP's site page gives grainy greywacke, weathered slate and clay slate that warm easily, among the hottest sites of the Ahr, south east to south west, 125 to 220 metres. Kept.
The making: the estate's own sheet gives spontaneous fermentation, twenty days on the skins, eighteen months on fine lees in barrique with thirty per cent new, six months in bottle, unfiltered.

tested: 1578 and 1900: several accounts (Wines of Germany, Meininger's profile, wine databases) give winegrowing since 1578 and 1900 as the house's founding year. Kept, hedged.

The Herrenberg: the house's page puts it beneath the Schwedenkopf rock, terraced in its southern part opposite the Saffenburg ruin; the VDP traces the name to the counts of Saffenburg, lords of Rech, and calls it the one Grosse Lage of Rech. Kept.
The Hardtberg Spätburgunder in others: Falstaff prints GG for 2014 and 2022, the house's own list an Erstes Gewächs.

tested: Sole ownership since 1714: the VDP's estate page; the house's pages give 1716. The story's early eighteenth century stands.
Size and the smallest claim: the house gives 0.68 hectare and the smallest single site in Germany, the VDP's site page 0.64; hedged as the family's, no size printed.
Ungrafted vines up to a hundred years old: the house's Weinlagen page and a merchant; the VDP says a part is ungrafted. Kept.
Used French barriques: the VDP's wine parcel of October 2020. Kept, hedged to 2020.
Kleine Kammer from the Gärkammer: a merchant's page and Falstaff's Walporzheim Kleine Kammer listing. Kept.
Soil: dark greywacke and weathered slate with sandy loam, steep and south facing, on the VDP's site page.

open: The size claim stays the family's: the house and the VDP's estate page quote the family calling the Gärkammer the smallest in Germany, one VDP summary says the smallest cru vineyard in Europe, and the VDP's site page gives 0.64 hectare against the house's 0.68; no size is printed.
The making for the Gärkammer itself (maceration, months in barrel) is in no source found; the record says only that the house favoured used French barriques, as the VDP described its cellar in 2020.
The younger generation's arrival in 2015 rests on the house's own team page.

tested: 1574: Caspar Cossmann and his wife in a debt register of Are castle, on wein.plus's glossary and the house's own history. Kept.
1868: Wines of Germany gives 20 December 1868, eighteen growers and the world's first wine growers' cooperative. Kept.
1952: Alfred Cossmann left the cooperative, wein.plus. Kept, unnamed for want of dates.
1980: wein.plus gives the new estate built and named Deutzerhof in 1980 because the Cossmann name would pass with the only daughter, who married a tax adviser in 1977. Rewritten.
2020: wein.plus gives the handover to a long standing friend of the family in 2020, the house's price list the same; Meininger 1 February. Kept.

The Mönchberg: the VDP gives 200 to 220 metres, south facing, greywacke with a little loam, slate terraces, the largest Grosse Lage of the Ahr, and the two abbeys, Deutz and Klosterrath. The trap of more than one Mönchberg stands: the VDP lists a Mönchberg at Stetten in Württemberg.

changed.now: in 1980 the family built a new estate at the foot of the Mönchberg and named it Deutzerhof, since the Cossmann name would pass with its only daughter; her husband turned the cellar to wild yeasts
changed.why: wein.plus dates the building and the name to 1980 and gives the reason; the son in law married in and qualified as a master grower only in 1982, so the move is the family's.

open: Wild yeast fermentation since the 1980s rests on the house's own account.
The sale of 2020 rests on the house's price list and wein.plus; Meininger gives 1 February without the year in the summary read.

tested: 1953: the house's front page and wein.plus (founded by the then managing clerk of the Dernau growers' cooperative). Kept.
1994 and 29: the house's history page. The man who ran the estate for more than forty years is called the founder by wein.plus's naming and the founder's son by the record; unsettled, so reworded.
VDP membership 2000: the house and the VDP. Kept.
Meckenheim and February 2024: the VDP's estate page gives the temporary address at Meckenheim, the house's history page the return of sales to Dernau at the end of February 2024. Kept.

The Hardtberg GG: the house's site, wein.plus and Falstaff (2009 to 2023) show a Frühburgunder GG only, the Spätburgunder GGs from the Schieferlay, Silberberg and Sonnenberg; the house names the Hardtberg in the upper Eigelstal among its top sites and says every one of its sites may give a Grosses Gewächs.

The fragment lints sound only once plan.json carries the accepted wine; tested here against a copy of the plan with that one change.

swaps.proposed: The author wrote the record for the Dernauer Hardtberg Frühburgunder GG and proposed changing the pick's wine in plan.json from Dernauer Hardtberg Spätburgunder GG, keeping the key and the producer.
swaps.why: The house's own Vinifizierung page, wein.plus's listings and Falstaff's listings from 2009 to 2023 show Kreuzberg's Hardtberg Grosses Gewächs as Frühburgunder only, with Gault Millau and Vinum placings for it on the house's site; its Spätburgunder GGs come from the Schieferlay, Silberberg and Sonnenberg, and the Hardtberg Spätburgunder GG that Falstaff lists belongs to Jean Stodden. The plan's wine does not exist as a Kreuzberg wine.

planEntry.why: the house's Hardtberg Grosses Gewächs is Frühburgunder, not Spätburgunder

swaps.forReadTogether: Set the pick's wine to Dernauer Hardtberg Frühburgunder GG in plan.json and record the swap in the group's swaps; the key kreuzberg stays, as the Pfalz ruling did. The pick's why (its Grosses Gewächs of Spätburgunder comes from the Hardtberg) must be rewritten to say Frühburgunder. With the wine changed, the fragment lints sound (tested here against a copy of the plan with that one change).
